paragraphs: The Trump administration has proposed new eligibility rules for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), the largest US food aid programme, that would remove about 6.3 million people, according to Al Jazeera. The US Department of Agriculture published the proposed rule on Tuesday. It would end automatic SNAP eligibility for households that qualify for another programme, Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF).

SNAP normally requires household income below 130 percent of the federal poverty level. TANF rules vary by state and can cover households earning up to 200 percent. The USDA said the revisions would ensure benefits are targeted to needy households while keeping the statutory purpose of simplifying program administration. The proposal is open for public comment for 30 days.

By the USDA's own figures, the change would remove about 17 percent of beneficiaries from a programme that currently enrolls more than 36 million people. It would also remove 1.8 million children from free school lunches, because they would no longer qualify. The average benefit is about $190 per person per month, or $356 per household.

Democrats criticised the plan. Representative Angie Craig said it would make it harder to meet basic needs and roll back efforts to streamline federal programs. Senator Cory Booker called it "despicable" and said Americans are already struggling with grocery prices. The article carried no response from the administration beyond the USDA's proposal.

Al Jazeera notes the proposal follows earlier changes. It says 5.5 million people already lost benefits under the July 2025 budget law, which expanded work requirements and made some immigrants ineligible. In December 2025 the administration threatened to withhold funding from 21 states that refused to share beneficiary data, which it said it needed to examine to cut fraud. The administration has said many recipients do not need the aid.

The United States again failed to appear at its United Nations human rights review in Geneva on Tuesday, according to NPR and Al Jazeera. Human Rights Council President Sidharto Reza Suryodipuro announced that the US delegation was not in the room. The council responded by delaying its examination of the US record until January.

The universal periodic review applies to all 193 UN member states, each of which is examined by fellow members every four to five years. NPR reports the US is the only member to skip it twice. Israel skipped a review in 2013 and returned nine months later after it was rescheduled. NPR says the UN has few sanctions available against a country that does not cooperate.

The State Department said Washington has withdrawn from the council, which Al Jazeera dates to February 2025. A spokesperson said taking part would imply endorsement of the council's work and called the body "irredeemable," accusing it of pushing "anti-American rhetoric." According to Al Jazeera, the spokesperson did not respond to allegations about the US record.

Jamil Dakwar of the American Civil Liberties Union, which led civil society groups to Geneva, cited the treatment of immigrants, student protesters and LGBTQ people as rights violations. Al Jazeera notes Washington maintains its deportations follow US immigration law. Nearly 200 submissions came from advocacy groups, and countries had planned to raise abortion access and the death penalty.

Rights groups want the review held anyway. NPR reports UN insiders fear that doing so without the US could set a risky precedent and encourage other states to stay away. Eric Tistounet of the Geneva Graduate Institute told Al Jazeera the walkout could damage the review system's credibility. Deliberations on how to respond are postponed until early next year.

A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed Monday found 71% of Americans want Congress to pass legislation ending the war with Iran, including 93% of Democrats and 51% of Republicans. The poll also found 62% would support repealing tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump, and nine in 10 said the cost of living should be a focus of Congress in its first 100 days. The poll surveyed 1,705 US adults online, with a margin of error of about 2 percentage points.

Democrats won their largest majorities in the Senate and House since at least 2008 in last week's midterms and take power when the new Congress is sworn in on January 3. Trump has defended the war as necessary to stop Iran acquiring a nuclear weapon and says tariffs will protect American industry. Democratic leaders have said they will address living costs and try to force an end to the war.

Large majorities in both parties said it was important for Trump and congressional Democrats to try to work together. On impeachment, 42% said an attempt would be bad for the country and 33% said it would be good. Democrats are divided on how aggressively to target Trump. A House impeachment vote on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is expected this week.

Al Jazeera notes that delivering on these priorities could be hard. Most Senate bills need 60 votes to overcome a filibuster, and Trump can veto legislation. Political scientist Seth Masket said voters want Democrats to fix problems and, to some extent, hold the administration accountable.

The poll put Trump's approval at 32%. Democrats were viewed favourably by 45% and unfavourably by 51%, while Republicans were viewed favourably by 35% and unfavourably by 60%. House Democrats hold leadership elections on November 18 and 19.

Police in Bangladesh fired tear gas and rubber bullets at supporters of deposed Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina on Tuesday, the BBC reports. In Gopalganj district, members of the banned student wing of her Awami League party, the Bangladesh Chhatra League (BCL), clashed with security forces, and a police vehicle was set on fire. The protests are seen as the first organised show of force by Hasina's supporters since she was ousted in August 2024.

The nationwide demonstrations began a day after Hasina said she had asked for a passport to return from exile in India. Protesters tried to block roads with burning tyres, and about 200 briefly blocked the Padma bridge. A 60-year-old bus driver died from smoke inhalation after a vehicle was set alight in Faridpur. Local media reported dozens of crude bombs exploding in recent days.

A BCL leader living in exile said supporters were not responsible for the violence and blamed "unknown miscreants." Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said attempts to create instability from across the border in India would not succeed.

Hasina fled to India after an uprising ended her 15-year rule. The United Nations has estimated up to 1,400 people were killed in the 2024 protests, mostly by gunfire from security forces. A special tribunal sentenced her to death in absentia last year for crimes against humanity. She denies the charges and calls the trial biased and politically motivated.

Hasina says she wants to return in December. The government said it will not issue her a passport and called her a fugitive. A junior foreign minister said Bangladesh wants India to hand her over under an extradition treaty. A state prosecutor said the verdict would be carried out if she returned. Awami League leaders allege hundreds of supporters have been killed; Dhaka officials reject claims that supporters are systematically targeted.

Malaysia's former prime minister Najib Razak returned to his Kuala Lumpur home late on Tuesday to serve the rest of a corruption sentence under house arrest, the BBC reports. The 73-year-old arrived from prison in an SUV escorted by a heavily armed police convoy, ending a four-year prison stint. His mansion was declared a federal prison ahead of the move.

Najib was convicted over the 1MDB scandal, in which investigators estimate $4.5bn was siphoned from the state-owned wealth fund he co-founded. Prosecutors say more than $1bn went to accounts linked to him. His lawyers say advisers misled him, particularly financier Jho Low, who maintains his innocence and remains at large. Najib denies wrongdoing.

He was first sentenced in 2020 to 12 years, over 42 million ringgit transferred from SRC International, a former 1MDB unit, and was jailed in 2022. The term was later halved on appeal. In September the King of Malaysia granted a conditional pardon allowing him to serve the remaining two years at home. His party paid a $12m fine as part of the pardon's terms.

The transfer had been due on Friday but was put on hold after the attorney general sought clarification of the royal decree. On Tuesday the high court ruled the house arrest was effective immediately. Critics said the release undermined anti-corruption efforts and questioned its legal basis, saying Malaysian law makes no provision for house arrest.

Najib is appealing a separate 15-year sentence handed down in December 2025 for misappropriating nearly 2.3 billion ringgit from 1MDB. He is due to begin serving that sentence after his house arrest ends, expected in August 2028.

Indonesian Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka offered to resign during a meeting with President Prabowo Subianto on Tuesday, according to officials, NPR reports. Raka, 39, is the son of former President Joko Widodo. State Secretariat Minister Prasetyo Hadi said the two held more than two hours of talks.

Hadi said it was not immediately clear whether Prabowo accepted the offer. He said the president advised Raka to continue pursuing legal avenues to defend the validity of his academic documents. Leaving his office later, Raka made a brief statement without addressing the resignation. He said he respects public criticism and does not want the situation to become a prolonged political controversy.

The offer comes amid growing pressure over a court dispute about his academic credentials. The controversy escalated last month after the Supreme Court ruled that the documents he submitted about his overseas education did not meet election requirements. The ruling fuelled calls from some lawmakers for his impeachment.

NPR says the resignation offer apparently was not related to a separate probe into allegations that top police officials were involved in a wiretap targeting the president. They include presidential chief of staff Gen. Listyo Sigit Prabowo, and three other police generals are also implicated. Listyo previously served as national police chief under Widodo, who has not been implicated in the investigation.

The developments come amid a widening political rift between Prabowo and Widodo, who backed Prabowo's presidential bid after Prabowo chose Raka as his running mate. Widodo faces unrelated allegations that he used a fake university diploma, which he denies.

Spain is bracing for a 24-hour general strike beginning at midnight on Wednesday over rents and the cost of living, Al Jazeera reports. The country's two biggest unions, CCOO and UGT, called it under the slogan "wages, housing, prices." They last called a general strike together in 2012. It is expected to disrupt transport, schools and healthcare, with flight cancellations and delays, though minimum services will be maintained in essential sectors.

The strike follows the September eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from her Madrid home after her corporate landlord raised the rent. She has since died. Images of her removal on a stretcher prompted nationwide protests and fed a political crisis that led the government to call snap elections for November 29.

The Bank of Spain estimates the country has 750,000 fewer homes than it needs, a gap that could exceed one million by 2028. According to the Spanish Youth Council, average rent is 1,176 euros a month, while a young person's average salary is 1,190 euros.

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has not explicitly endorsed the strike but praised collective action as the source of social gains such as pensions and public healthcare. The opposition Popular Party and far-right Vox dismissed the strike as politically motivated and criticised its timing, a day after the state funeral for victims of a train crash that killed 69 people. Analyst Luke Stobart said the strike keeps housing at the centre of the campaign.

The Socialists have lost support amid corruption scandals involving Sanchez's inner circle and family members, and the Popular Party leads polls and could govern with Vox. Stobart said it is unclear whether union leaders and the government can control the narrative, and warned the protests could grow and backfire on the government.

Parents of student athletes in Washington state have sued to block a ballot initiative banning transgender girls from girls' sports teams, The Guardian reports. Voters passed Initiative 638 last week. The suit, filed in state court on Monday, calls the measure discriminatory and warns it would lead to invasive genital examinations of female athletes.

The plaintiffs are parents of transgender and cisgender girls, the advocacy group TransFamilies, and the Washington Education Association teachers' union. They are represented by the ACLU of Washington, Legal Voice and Pacifica Law Group. The Guardian reports that Nebraska, Colorado and Arizona adopted similar sports bans, though advocates say Washington's is particularly extreme.

The measure requires girls to provide medical documentation of their sex before joining girls' teams, through hormone or genetic tests or an examination of their reproductive anatomy. It does not apply to boys and covers elementary, middle and high school students. The lawsuit argues it violates the state constitution, including privacy and equal rights protections, and a state anti-discrimination law protecting transgender people.

Proponents, according to the Guardian, argue the ban protects fairness in girls' sports. It was funded by conservative hedge fund manager Brian Heywood. Legal Voice's Tiffani Lennon said Washington has let trans youth play on teams matching their gender for 20 years, and called the issue manufactured. School officials said earlier this year they knew of about 10 trans athletes among roughly 200,000 student athletes statewide.
The Seattle public schools board voted Monday to allow the district to take legal action against the ban. The measure is due to take effect on December 3.

Consumer prices rose a seasonally adjusted 0.4% in October, more than economists expected, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Tuesday. CNBC said economists surveyed by Dow Jones had forecast 0.3%. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, rose 0.3% against a forecast of 0.2%. In September, headline prices rose 0.6% and core rose 0.3%.

The BLS did not estimate a yearly rate. According to CNBC, last year's government shutdown kept the bureau from collecting enough data in October 2025, so there is no comparable figure. Energy rose 0.7% and gasoline 1%, even though gasoline prices have fallen in recent weeks. Food rose 0.5%, with beef up 0.9%. Transportation services rose 0.8%, electricity 0.9% and shelter 0.3%, which the BLS said accounted for more than 30% of the headline increase. Used cars and trucks fell 1.2%.

The data bears on the Federal Reserve's next move. At its October meeting, officials voted 10-2 to hold the benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4%. Fed Governor Christopher Waller said Tuesday that a hot report could push him toward favoring a half-point increase in December. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said she sees a need for two more quarter-point increases.

According to CME Group's FedWatch tool, traders fully price in a quarter-point increase at the Dec. 8-9 meeting and put the odds of a half-point move at 13.6%. Stocks fell and Treasury yields rose after the release. A net 37% of businesses in a National Federation of Independent Business survey said they plan to raise prices within three months, the highest share since July 2022. Logan said she is concerned the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, due later in November, could also come in higher.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday called impeachment articles against him a politically motivated "farce," in his first Pentagon press briefing since May 5, according to Defense News. The session lasted under 25 minutes and he took few questions. Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky introduced eight articles on Monday.

Massie accuses Hegseth of, among other things, taking the country to war with Iran without congressional authorization, continuing it past War Powers Resolution timelines, directing the seizure of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, ordering deadly strikes on suspected drug boats, and retaliating against Sen. Mark Kelly. Hegseth called the accusations "partisan policy disagreements" and said every operation was lawful, ordered by the president and notified to Congress.

Vice President JD Vance wrote on X that the question of whether Hegseth committed impeachable crimes is "absurd." He said lawmakers were targeting Hegseth because he took on Pentagon bureaucracy, not because of Iran. Defense News said Vance had blamed the war for Republicans' midterm losses. President Trump called Massie a "loser" on Monday.

Fox News reported that Democrats are backing the effort. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said he is a "hard yes." Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said the Senate should put Hegseth on trial over what he called a failure in Iran. Rep. Gregory Meeks said Democrats would keep digging. Massie said his resolution is a gentler version of what Democrats will bring in January.

Defense News said the House has two legislative days to vote, and Speaker Mike Johnson decides whether the articles are voted on individually or together. A simple House majority would send the matter to the Senate, where conviction needs two-thirds.

Democrat Mary Peltola leads Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by 2,517 first-choice votes in Alaska's Senate race after Monday's ballot count, Fox News reported. As of Tuesday midday ET, Peltola had 48.6% (106,321 votes) and Sullivan 47.5% (103,804). Republican Gerald Heikes had 2.2% and independent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. had 1.7%. Roughly 75% to 76% of the expected vote is counted, and the race remains too close to call.

The lead has widened from a 637-vote edge that held for days after Election Day. Peltola campaign manager Cheryl Bruce said in a statement that Peltola "will be elected" once every vote is counted and that Peltola won Monday's batch 68-30.

Because no candidate has 50%, Alaska's ranked-choice system could come into play. Fox said Sullivan and President Trump have suggested the Republican would gain from later rounds. Fox's own account says the other Dan Sullivan would be eliminated first, which might help Peltola pass 50%.

Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.'s candidacy, dubbed "Decoy Dan," is under review. Gov. Mike Dunleavy said the state is investigating whether there was wrongdoing, and some Republicans allege it was meant to draw votes from the incumbent. Fox did not report a response from Sullivan Jr.
Dunleavy said large ballot counts are expected Nov. 13 and Nov. 18. The official ranked-choice tabulation is set for Nov. 18, after the overseas absentee deadline, and certification for Nov. 25.
Fox reported that Democrats hold a 54-44 Senate edge with Alaska and Mississippi still undecided, where Democrat Scott Colom leads Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by about 2,500 votes.

Russian and Ukrainian delegations held about four hours of U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, the first such session since February, according to the BBC and NPR. A second day is scheduled for Wednesday. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who did not attend, called the talks "constructive and quite substantive." Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking in Paris, called them "very productive" but urged patience, saying the issue is not close to being solved.

Zelensky said the talks centered on humanitarian issues, including prisoner exchanges, captive civilians and children taken from Ukraine, and also covered security guarantees. A senior Ukrainian official told NPR a large prisoner swap was discussed, with details to come.

The U.S. team included Jared Kushner and envoy Steve Witkoff. Kushner said the U.S. had "narrowed the gaps" between the sides, without giving details. The BBC reported that the Ukrainians first met European and NATO officials, which Russia has objected to, though Moscow said EU representatives could join later.

Positions remain far apart. According to the BBC, Moscow demands that Ukraine give up the parts of Donetsk it holds, while Kyiv wants to freeze the current line. A U.S. official said both sides had shown "a little bit of flexibility, privately." Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov rejected a ceasefire, saying it would let Kyiv regroup. NPR said Putin also demands that Ukraine abandon its NATO bid.
The BBC noted that Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko said he believes Trump wants a quick deal at Ukraine's expense. Kushner said the talks could at most build momentum toward the next phase.

Anthropic said in an updated filing on Tuesday that it will offer 825 million shares at $70 to $78 each in its planned Nasdaq IPO. CNBC and TechCrunch reported that the sale could raise $57.75 billion to $64.35 billion. At the top of the range, the company could be worth about $1.4 trillion on a fully diluted basis, up from the $965 billion valuation it announced in May. CNBC, citing people familiar, said pricing is planned for Nov. 18 and trading Nov. 19 under the ticker "ANT."

Anthropic also agreed to sell $26 billion of non-voting Class N stock privately at the IPO price to AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC. TechCrunch said Google and Nvidia are each investing $10 billion. About 20% of the offering is targeted at retail investors, CNBC's sources said, well above the typical 5% to 10%.

The filing says nine-month revenue was about $33.2 billion and the net loss was $104 billion. CNBC said most of that loss came from changes in the fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Run-rate revenue reached roughly $81 billion at the end of October.

The valuation is below earlier hopes. TechCrunch said the company had reportedly targeted $2 trillion, and CNBC reported that some investors doubted even $1.5 trillion. CNBC cited a more skeptical public market and a political climate shaped by last week's midterms. Its sources said institutional demand is already covering the range.
Founders hold a share class with 50.1% of voting power, per TechCrunch, so Class A buyers will have limited influence.

Anthropic's seven co-founders each plan to sell 3,378,378 shares in the company's IPO, according to the company's new S-1 filing, as reported by TechCrunch. At the midpoint of the $70 to $78 price range, $74, each would receive just under $250 million. At $70, each would take in a little over $236 million, and at $78, just under $264 million.

The sellers are CEO Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish and Christopher Olah. TechCrunch noted that the seven left OpenAI in 2021 after disagreements with its leadership over how AI should be built.

The sales would not end their control. After the offering, each founder will own about 3.2% of outstanding Class A shares, or roughly 22% together, the S-1 says. TechCrunch stressed that this is not their share of the whole company, because Class A is one of several classes. Others, including Amazon and Google, hold non-voting Class N shares, so the founders' stake in total equity will be considerably smaller.

Each founder will also receive one share of Class F stock, which carries supervoting rights. Together they would control 51.1% of the votes, and no single founder would hold significantly more shares or votes than the others, according to TechCrunch.

The filing also hints at demand, TechCrunch said. Board member Reed Hastings has indicated he wants to buy $300 million of shares through his donor-advised fund, and board member Christopher Liddell wants to buy $3 million. TechCrunch added that companies in heavily anticipated IPOs can often price shares above the initial range.

Nvidia's independent board members said Tuesday that they have hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, led by former acting U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York Joon H. Kim, to investigate CEO Jensen Huang, CNBC reported. The review will look at whether company secrets or national security were compromised. Kim joined the firm last month, according to Law360.

The investigation follows Huang's admission, in an email to staff on Sunday, of an affair with Alice Huang, a woman connected to Chinese intelligence. "My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did," he wrote, adding that he is an American and supports U.S. national security. An Nvidia representative said at the time that he intends to keep serving as CEO without interruption.

CNBC said The New York Times and Financial Times have reported that U.S. intelligence agencies surveilled Alice Huang, an Asian technology executive affiliated with Nvidia customer Megaspeed, and concluded that she passes information to Beijing. Nvidia's board said Sunday that it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised.

Investors have reacted sharply. Nvidia shares fell 6% on Tuesday after dropping more than 4% on Monday, as investors worry the scandal could force Huang out. CNBC also said Nvidia and its board face pressure from critics and politicians over what the company knew about sales of restricted AI chips to Chinese companies. The story was still developing when CNBC published it.

British counter-terrorism police have arrested a 41-year-old senior U.S. Army soldier on suspicion of offenses under the National Security Act, according to The Guardian and the BBC. He was arrested near Gloucester on Tuesday and remains in custody at a London police station. The BBC described the case as suspected spying for Russia. The Guardian said he has alleged links to Russia. Police have not named him.

Counter Terrorism Policing London said he was held under sections one and three of the National Security Act 2023. The BBC explained that section one covers obtaining or disclosing protected information and section three covers assisting a foreign intelligence service. The act allows police to hold a suspect without charge for up to 14 days. Officers are searching two locations in Gloucestershire.

Both outlets reported that the soldier was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, which the BBC said houses the headquarters of NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps. Police said the case is not linked to other counter-terrorism investigations.

FBI Director Kash Patel said the arrest "involves allegations of espionage" and that the FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath. Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command called the alleged conduct of a soldier entrusted with sensitive information "a sobering reminder that insider threats are real."
Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans said the allegations are serious and the investigation is ongoing. Police are working with U.S. authorities, the U.S. military, the FBI and MI5.

The Republican-led House Oversight Committee on Tuesday released its final report on the federal handling of investigations into Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell, ending a 15-month inquiry. The BBC reported that the report concludes Epstein's crimes after 2005 could have been prevented but for failures by federal investigators and prosecutors, including a 2007 agreement with the U.S. attorney's office in southern Florida that let him avoid federal prosecution.

The committee said it conducted 19 transcribed interviews and seven depositions. It found that the Justice Department communicated poorly about document releases and that deficient redactions exposed survivors' sensitive information. It also said questions remain about whether all relevant documents were released. On Epstein's 2019 death, the report cited institutional failures at the jail but said testimony could not definitively dispel certain theories.

Chairman James Comer urged the department to interview key witnesses, investigate associates accused of crimes and give survivors access to their records. A Justice Department spokesperson said the recommendations "have already been addressed" and that the case is not closed.

Democrats dispute the report. Rep. Robert Garcia, the committee's top Democrat, called it "misleading" and "partisan," said it rests on an incomplete investigation with no public hearings, and accused the department of withholding over 2.5 million pages. The BBC said the report accuses Democrats of trying to implicate President Trump, and that the committee's document review found nothing implicating him. Trump's name appears thousands of times in the files, but the BBC noted that this does not imply wrongdoing.
Democrats take over the committee in January. Garcia said they intend to hold public hearings, including questions about Trump.

French police have made arrests after searching three properties, including the Ritz hotel in Paris, in an investigation into sexual abuse and trafficking linked to the late Mohamed Al Fayed, the Paris public prosecutor's office said. Several people were taken into custody last month and later released. The BBC reports these are the first arrests over the alleged abuse and trafficking.

The prosecutor's office said searches took place in mid-October at the Ritz, the Villa Sainte-Thérèse in Saint-Tropez and the Villa Windsor in Paris, with British investigators present. The Metropolitan Police told survivors its officers attended on 13 and 14 October. French prosecutors described a preliminary investigation into alleged human trafficking and aggravated pimping by an organised group, and rape. Seized digital material is being analysed, and several alleged victims have been interviewed.

Al Fayed died in 2023 aged 94. More than 20 women accused him of sexual assault in a BBC documentary and podcast in 2024, and the BBC says more than 400 alleged victims or witnesses have since contacted lawyers. Survivors' groups cited by the Guardian put the figure above 500, and the Guardian says the Met is investigating 169 victims.

Survivor groups welcomed the searches but asked for more. Justice for Fayed and Harrods Survivors urged equal thoroughness at every property, including in Britain. No One Above said the National Crime Agency should take over the investigation from the Met; the Met's reply to that call was not reported. The Ritz Paris told AFP it does not tolerate harassment, abuse or inappropriate behaviour and will cooperate fully with judicial authorities.

Britain and Argentina have clashed at the international tribunal for the law of the sea in Hamburg over the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falkland Islands. Argentina is seeking a provisional ruling that would suspend drilling, which it says poses an environmental risk, before further arbitration. The Guardian reports the hearing is sitting over two days.

Argentina argues that UK approval of the project breaches a 1976 UN resolution calling on both sides to avoid unilateral action while the sovereignty dispute is unsettled. Mario Oyarzábal, chief legal adviser to Argentina's foreign ministry, told the tribunal that islanders have no right to decide which state the islands belong to, and that the resources belong to the Argentine people. He said Argentina is ready to negotiate all aspects of the question, and that Argentina, not the UK, would bear the consequences of a spill.

UK attorney general Ellie Reeves said Argentina is using the application to pursue its sovereignty claim. She said suspending drilling, due to start in March, would kill the project and cost the islanders billions of pounds, and cited their right to self-determination. UK lawyers said the risk of an incident is low and the companies have mitigated it. Sir Michael Wood KC said provisional measures should be used only in exceptional circumstances. Asked whether the UK would abide by a ruling, Reeves said she respected the tribunal but would not get ahead of its decisions.

The project, led by Navitas with Rockhopper, would produce oil from 2028 for 35 years and could double the islands' GDP per capita. Argentina's president, Javier Milei, has condemned it as unlawful. The Guardian says it is the first time substantive matters about the islands have been litigated at an international tribunal. The hearing continues on Wednesday.

The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in London, the final court of appeal for Trinidad and Tobago, has overturned laws criminalising same-sex intimacy in the country. The ruling came in a case brought by activist Jason Jones, 62, whose legal fight has lasted around a decade; the BBC calls it 11 years and the Guardian 10. The judges found the laws could not be reasonably justified in a society that properly respects individual rights, according to Lord Sales.

Jones first won in Trinidad's High Court in 2018, when Judge Devindra Rampersad found the colonial-era provisions on anal sex unconstitutional. The government appealed and in 2025 the Court of Appeal reversed that decision, finding the provisions were protected by a "savings clause" shielding older inherited laws. The Privy Council's five judges unanimously disagreed, the Guardian reports, finding that the 1986 Sexual Offences Act was new legislation and so not protected. The BBC says the Attorney General had argued the savings clause barred such challenges.

The court upheld Rampersad's remedy, which makes anal sex legal between consenting adults of any gender over 16 and also decriminalises same-sex intimacy, referred to in the 1925 act as "gross indecency".

Campaigners say the ruling could reach beyond Trinidad. The BBC says it is the first time the Privy Council has decided such a case, and that some 34 Commonwealth countries still criminalise homosexuality. Jones said the judgment would have a "domino effect" across countries that use the Privy Council as their top court, but also said it might be decades before its benefits are seen in daily life. A lawyer in St Vincent and the Grenadines, where a High Court judge upheld similar laws in 2024, said the decision should influence litigation there. Pride TT welcomed the ruling but said discrimination in work, housing and healthcare remains.

Russian naval activity around the UK rose by 41% in the first nine months of the year, a British defence minister has said. Luke Pollard, the minister for defence readiness, called it "a huge increase" as the Royal Navy announced plans to step up a 10-country maritime defensive effort, the Northern Navies Initiative, according to the Guardian.

Under the plan, sea drones from the UK and other countries would work interchangeably with warships from across the group, which includes the Netherlands and the Baltic and Nordic countries. Pollard said a British drone could be teamed with a British, Danish or Norwegian warship and handed off to an allied ship. A further £90m will go to underwater drones and sensors to monitor the Greenland-Iceland-UK gap for Russian submarines.

Pollard said Russian spy ships such as the Yantar have sailed near UK waters seeking a better picture of critical infrastructure and mapping undersea cables. Russian frigates have escorted tankers in the North Sea and Channel, and in June fired shots near a pleasure yacht south of the Isle of Wight. Pollard said Russia-linked tankers now often sail around the UK after the seizure of one, the Smyrtos.

The plan comes as British frigate numbers could fall from 12 in 2021 to three by 2030. Last month the cross-party defence select committee warned that shortfalls in ships and submarines risk weakening deterrence. Pollard blamed past Conservative governments for cutting budgets and delaying investment; a Conservative response was not reported. He said an extra £10bn a year for defence by 2030, announced in October's budget, lets the UK send a clear demand signal to industry. He said the Royal Navy is "ready to fight tonight".

Russian cargo ships have carried military equipment including tanks, armored vehicles and rocket launchers to African ports that serve as gateways for Moscow's forces on the continent, according to a new investigation by C4ADS, a Washington-based group that tracks illicit networks. The findings were shared with Defense News ahead of public release on Nov. 10.

The analysts followed a sample of a dozen ships with operational ties to Russian military shipments between 2023 and 2026, using ship transponder data, satellite imagery, on-the-ground pictures and local reporting. They said the ports of Conakry in Guinea, Tobruk in Libya and Lomé in Togo were particularly important for logistics likely supporting Russia's Africa Corps, which grew out of the Wagner Group. Mali, a hot spot for the Corps, may have been the final destination for many of the weapons.

C4ADS said the ships Adler and Siyanie Severa reached Conakry in January 2025, and within days a convoy of roughly a hundred military vehicles, including MRAP armored vehicles and T-72 tanks, was filmed arriving in Bamako, Mali's capital. It said the cargo ship Mikhail Britnev likely carried vehicles to Lomé in mid-2026, after which Malian state television showed 29 armored vehicles in Bamako that reporters said had come from Lomé. Some ships were escorted by Russian warships and often switched off tracking signals.

The researchers also flagged the port of Pointe-Noire in the Republic of Congo as a possible new hub, noting that three U.S.-sanctioned vehicle carriers traveled there, but said more work is needed to establish the nature of those shipments. C4ADS said ten of the twelve vessels are U.S.-sanctioned, six are covered by British sanctions and five by European Union sanctions. Defense News says the sea routes complement an air network it has previously investigated.

France has ordered two military Earth-observation satellites from Airbus and Thales Alenia Space in a contract worth more than €1.5 billion, about $1.7 billion. The satellites are part of the IRIS system and will replace three existing orbiters, according to France's Directorate General of Armament, known as the DGA, which announced the order on Monday.

The DGA said the new satellites will outperform the current CSO satellites in image quality and in how quickly images become available. They are to take extremely high-resolution images day and night, in visible and infrared light, anywhere in the world. The first is planned to become operational in 2033, with both in orbit around 2035. The three CSO satellites were launched in 2018, 2020 and 2025.

Airbus said it will provide the satellite platforms and the ground segment, along with a significant share of the first satellite's payload. Thales Alenia Space will develop the second payload and provide key elements of the first. Thales, which owns 67% of Thales Alenia Space with Italy's Leonardo holding the rest, said the first IRIS satellite will replace CSO-1 and CSO-2, and the second will improve resolution once the last CSO reaches the end of its life. The DGA said it notified the companies on Nov. 5.

Defense News notes France is one of few European NATO members with its own constellation of high-end optical spy satellites, and that President Emmanuel Macron said in January France was providing two thirds of the intelligence capabilities supplied to Ukraine. The system will be run by the Space Command within the French Air and Space Force, and the DGA said the program is open to cooperation so partner countries can gain access.

The U.S. Air Force's semi-autonomous Collaborative Combat Aircraft have flown in formation and carried out air combat maneuvers for the first time, according to a recent release from Shield, the company behind their autonomy software.

Shield's Hivemind software helped multiple CCAs fly in a multi-ship formation and execute beyond-visual-range counter-air tactics during an Oct. 26 exercise. The release did not say how many aircraft took part or which CCA type was involved. Todd Wesley, Shield's vice president of Hivemind engineering, said the aircraft and mission systems are reaching a level of integration that lets the company start showing what Hivemind can do.

Each flight generates data that feeds into a software release, which supports decisions on testing and fielding, the statement said. Wesley said the combined Hivemind and aircraft release process is nearing the point where the Air Force can fly a sortie, update the software overnight and fly again the next day.

The Air Force has announced its intention to have 500 combat-ready semi-autonomous systems by 2032, with an overall fleet of 1,000. Its fiscal 2027 budget request for the CCA program includes $996.5 million in procurement, $150 million in advanced procurement for the following year and $1.37 billion in continued research and development, for a total of $2.37 billion.

Last month an F-22 Raptor completed airborne tactical command and in-flight control of a YFQ-44A, acting as a "quarterback" that gave high-level directives to the Anduril-made aircraft. Separately, Shield AI said last week it will acquire Echodyne, which makes solid-state radar systems, in a $5.3 billion transaction.

Amazon's Ring has unveiled two robots: the $250 Ring Drone Cam for homes and the $1,000 Ring Rover Cam for businesses. Both fall under a new Ring Robotics brand, according to Wired. CNBC reports the company announced them on Tuesday.

The textbook-sized Drone Cam flies from room to room, including upstairs, and films by day or night. When a sensor or alarm on a window, door or other security device is triggered, it follows a preset path to investigate. It flies up to eight minutes before returning to its dock. Ring CEO Jamie Siminoff said its built-in lights and loud propellers can work as a deterrent. Wired reports its intelligence runs in the cloud, which keeps the drone light. Siminoff said it cannot fly outside, in line with Federal Aviation Administration rules. It ships Jan. 27, pending Federal Communications Commission approval.

The Rover Cam repurposes hardware from Amazon's Astro home robot, with a display on a two-wheeled base, an extendable periscope camera, a siren, two-way audio and a light tower. Aimed at offices, warehouses and other workplaces, it ships Dec. 16. Wired notes Amazon previously sold Astro to businesses for $2,350 before ending support for the device.

Ring says privacy is the default mode and that the devices flash an LED when recording. Wired reports Ring temporarily holds encryption keys to run cloud AI features, which makes the system less strict than true end-to-end encryption. Ring has faced privacy concerns over its police partnerships, and CNBC says it canceled an integration with Flock Safety this year. Thorin Klosowski of the Electronic Frontier Foundation told Wired buyers should think through how such a device would make others in the home feel.

Axon Enterprise said last week it has invested $1.2 billion in drone maker Skydio, giving it 20% ownership of a company valued at $5.2 billion, The Robot Report says. Skydio is based in San Mateo, California, and Axon in Scottsdale, Arizona.

Axon will also become Skydio's exclusive distributor for public safety in the U.S. and Canada, and the companies said they will work together to bring Skydio drones to more agencies. Axon is expanding its Drone as First Responder, or DFR, program, in which drones are sent to calls. Skydio said it serves more than 1,500 public safety customers, and that more than 28 million Americans live within two miles of a DFR dock.

Axon said that at agencies using Skydio DFR, priority response times have fallen by as much as 65%, and drones arrive before officers on about 80% of the calls where they are deployed. The companies said that earlier visibility can help de-escalate dangerous situations and locate missing people. These are company claims, and the report offers no independent verification.

The investment is a mix of cash and Axon stock, and includes both new capital for Skydio and the purchase of shares from existing shareholders. Skydio plans to use part of the cash to speed up product development. Axon estimates the DFR market at about $13 billion in the U.S. and Canada, and Skydio expects about $1 billion in total bookings this fiscal year. Axon expects the transactions to close in the fourth quarter of 2026 and the first quarter of 2027, subject to customary conditions. The report adds that delivery-drone company Zipline raised $1.5 billion last week.

Google DeepMind has released Gemini Robotics 2.5, a new version of its AI platform for robots, along with an open safety benchmark called ASIMOV-Jailbreak, Ars Technica reports. The platform pairs a reasoning model that plans tasks from live video with a vision-language-action model that generates the robot's movements.

DeepMind says version 2.5 is much better at dexterous tasks. It was evaluated across more than 200 activities, including serving food with tongs and using a pipette, and Apptronik's Apollo 2 humanoid with the model could tie a bow. Compared with the previous version, DeepMind reports a 30 to 100 percent higher success rate and 20 to 30 percent faster performance in lab testing. In European Mercedes-Benz factories, Apollo 2 robots kitted automotive parts with a 96 percent success rate. DeepMind director Kanishka Rao called closing the remaining 4 percent gap a "steep road".

The team says another Google model, Gemini 4 Argon, helped build a simulation engine that generated variations of practice runs from real camera data, speeding development. The model still runs on cloud servers, so latency remains. DeepMind says reasoning at inference time lets the robot stop or wait when hazards appear, and that robots completed tasks safely 33 percent more often with obstacles present and 43 percent more often when people were in the way.

ASIMOV-Jailbreak is an open dataset of 1,500 prompts meant to trick a robot into unsafe actions. DeepMind says using Argon in the loop gives a 98.8 percent jailbreak safety level, against 73.5 percent for Gemini Robotics ER 2 alone. The dataset is on Hugging Face. Gemini Robotics 2.5 is not generally available but is with partners including Agile Robots, Apptronik and Boston Dynamics.

Google on Monday unveiled two new variants of its tensor processing units, or TPUs, the in-house chips it designs for AI workloads, TechCrunch reported. The chips, called TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max, extend the company's eighth-generation lineup, introduced in April, to confidential model training and to workloads that need more memory.

TPU 8tx was designed with AMD and is based on the TPU 8t chip. Google said in a blog post that it is meant for confidentially training and running AI models, and that it "builds security directly into the hardware layer, keeping sensitive data and model weights protected and isolated even while in active use."

According to the report, the chip also has a custom inferencing network that lets it run reasoning alongside training, so it can distill and train small models on the fly. Google said this could help companies that want to train a model on proprietary data without moving the data between devices.

TPU 8i Max combines two of the inference-focused TPU 8i chips launched in April in a single package, doubling memory capacity, processing power and bandwidth. The result, TechCrunch said, lets AI models handle a larger range of information during queries.

TechCrunch framed the launch as part of Google's effort to reduce its dependence on chips made by other companies for its cloud computing business. It also noted that Microsoft, Amazon, OpenAI and Anthropic are working on their own AI-specific semiconductors and software to reduce reliance on Nvidia's dominance.

Remote access company N-able has taken its cloud-hosted N-Central offering offline after a security researcher published a set of previously unknown vulnerabilities, known as zero-days, online, TechCrunch reported. The publication gave the company no advance notice to fix them.

In a status update, N-able said the hosted service is offline "while we take the necessary actions to secure the environments and implement appropriate remediation." It also urged customers to take down their own self-hosted N-Central deployments, fearing attackers could use the publicly disclosed exploits to break into customer networks.

N-Central lets corporate customers remotely access and manage other devices and systems on the same network, and N-able said customers cannot use the service during the outage. TechCrunch noted that remote access technologies are a frequent target of hackers because they can grant wide access to a company's network and internal data.

Researcher Ben Bales released the bugs on GitHub on Sunday. In a post on X he called them Able2Shell and described them as a mix of flaws capable of stealing credentials, creating new administrative accounts and gaining root access to affected N-able systems. He told Bleeping Computer he published them because the company allegedly failed to patch flaws he had reported in a different product.

N-able said it has no evidence of successful exploitation against any customer environment. A spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment on whether the company can check, for example through server logs, or has no way to check. The report did not give a timeline for restoring the service.

Oura announced on Tuesday that it is acquiring Counsel Health, an AI-native primary care company, for $625 million, TechCrunch reported. The deal comes a few weeks after Oura postponed its IPO of up to $2.2 billion indefinitely, citing "uncertainty in the IPO market."

Counsel Health runs a platform that combines a chat-based medical experience with access to licensed physicians. Its service was integrated into the Oura app in June. STAT described it as a chatbot users can talk with about health concerns before being transferred to a clinician for treatment and diagnosis over telehealth. The companies plan to expand their partnership across preventative care, acute care, and specialty and chronic care.

Oura CEO Tom Hale said in a press release that Oura helps members understand their physiology and that with Counsel they can act on their health, from quick questions and prescriptions to lab results, chronic care and referrals. Counsel CEO Muthu Alagappan said the company built its medical AI around trust, safety and responsibility, keeping physicians in the loop for clinical decisions.

Alagappan will become Oura's chief clinical AI officer, alongside Counsel's 70 employees, Bloomberg reported. Counsel will keep serving enterprise partners, with the goal of reaching people beyond Oura's membership. Counsel raised a $25 million Series A a year ago, and PitchBook estimates it had raised $36 million in total.

TechCrunch said the deal is expected to close before the end of 2027. Oura also reported revenue of $533 million for the quarter ended September 30, up 153% from a year earlier, and about $1.75 billion for fiscal 2026. STAT said the deal reflects a growing desire to connect wearables to clinical care.

A voluntary global target to raise electricity's share of final energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035 is among the key items at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, New Scientist reported. The target is based on analysis by the International Energy Agency and the International Renewable Energy Agency. Electricity is currently estimated at 23.4 percent of energy delivered to consumers, so meeting it would require the pace of electrification to quadruple compared with the first quarter of this century.

Researchers quoted by New Scientist differed in emphasis. Judit Hecke of New Climate Institute said acceleration is possible but depends on getting policy, investment and infrastructure moving together, and noted the target counts electricity however it is generated. Jan Rosenow of the University of Oxford called it broadly the right level of ambition and achievable, as electric options are often the cheapest. IRENA said the target alone will not be enough to meet temperature goals.

New Scientist noted that the US has withdrawn from the global climate framework and will be the only major economy absent from the talks, and that the UK, which supports the target, is reportedly expected to weaken its electric vehicle targets.

Separately, former US secretary of state John Kerry told the Guardian that China is the only country that has "hugely accelerated" its shift from fossil fuels and that others, including the US, should follow. He said that since the war in Iran and the interruption of the Strait of Hormuz, other countries have also moved to deploy more renewables. The Guardian reported that China has said it wants COP31 to discuss the free flow of green technology, widely seen as a reference to US and EU tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles and solar products. The US response to Kerry's comments was not reported.

On Wednesday, Nov. 18, NASA's Voyager 1 will reach a distance of one light-day from Earth, the agency said. That is more than 16 billion miles, or 25.9 billion kilometers, and means any light sent from Earth would take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft. Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object.

NASA is marking the milestone with two events. On Tuesday, Nov. 17, it invites people around the world to take part in "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day," creating a symbolic wave of golden light around the planet after sunset. NASA built a website that lets smartphones and tablets flash "VGR," Voyager's call sign, in Morse code. Participants are encouraged to photograph or film their signal and share it on social platforms, tagging @NASA.

On Thursday, Nov. 19, at 12 p.m. EST, NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California will host a moderated discussion with mission members and NASA leadership. Topics include the status of Voyager 1 and 2, the science the probes continue to gather in interstellar space, and the challenges of keeping them running at such distances. A question-and-answer session will follow, along with a preview of a NASA+ Voyager documentary planned for 2027, the mission's 50th anniversary.

Participants include Nicky Fox of NASA's Science Mission Directorate, JPL chief scientist Jonathan Lunine, Voyager project manager Suzanne Dodd, mission manager Kareem Badaruddin and deputy project scientist Jamie Rankin. U.S. media must RSVP by Nov. 16 to attend in person, and foreign national media by Nov. 12.
NASA noted that Voyager 1 entered interstellar space in 2012 and Voyager 2 followed in 2018. Both continue to provide observations of the environment beyond the heliosphere.

Several recent studies suggest the errors that quantum error-correction techniques must handle are more complex than expected, New Scientist reported. Quantum computers will not be useful until such methods are perfected, and the findings pose new challenges for making the machines practical.

A long-standing assumption, the Markov assumption, holds that qubit errors are memoryless, meaning errors at different times are uncorrelated. Lorenza Viola of Dartmouth College said memory effects would mean repeating the same operation could give different results depending on what the environment remembers. The report says memory effects keep appearing in experiments.

Ioan Pop at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology and colleagues developed a measurement method that found very long-lived defects in a superconducting qubit's environment, each of which could act as a memory. Earlier this year, Rami Barends of Forschungszentrum Jülich and colleagues found similar violations in a different type of qubit. A 2025 analysis of an error-correction experiment on Google's Willow computer found some hard-to-correct errors matched a non-Markovian model, and Gregory Quiroz of Johns Hopkins and colleagues found a model including such effects represented an IBM machine seven times better than commonly used noise models. IBM and Google did not respond to New Scientist's request for comment.

Viola also found that parts of the environment that remember can act as quantum systems and respond to a qubit, introducing a new kind of error current methods do not account for. She said the work is preliminary.

Kavan Modi said it is too early to sound the alarm but that no guarantees exist that the problem will not worsen as qubit numbers grow. Mathematical theorems suggest fault tolerance is possible despite correlated errors, but how strong correlations can be remains open, Viola said. Amit Hagar of Indiana University Bloomington said standard methods might work only for computations of limited length or complexity, and that the burden of proof now shifts to firms building the machines.
